body.heading: A shortcut in the wiring
paragraphs: Most messages in your body travel to the brain, which decides what to do. A reflex takes a shortcut. When sensors in your skin detect something harmful, the signal races along a nerve to your spinal cord — and the spinal cord sends back an order to move immediately, without waiting for the brain.

This loop is called a reflex arc, and it can complete in a fraction of a second. The signal still reaches your brain, which is why you feel the pain and think 'that was hot' — but by then, your hand is already safe.

body.heading: The famous knee tap
paragraphs: Doctors test this wiring with a small hammer tap just below the kneecap. The tap stretches a tendon, sensors report the stretch, and the spinal cord orders the thigh muscle to contract. The lower leg kicks, all by itself.
The point of that reflex is everyday balance: it constantly corrects small stretches in your muscles so you can stand and walk without thinking about every adjustment.

body.heading: Built-in first aid
paragraphs: You are born with many reflexes: blinking when something flies at your eyes, coughing when something irritates your throat, and pulling away from pain. They are not clever, and they are not always right — but they are fast, and in an emergency, fast is what matters.
Thinking is your brain's great gift. Reflexes are its humble bodyguards, standing watch while the thinking catches up.

takeaway: A reflex is a spinal-cord shortcut that moves your body first and lets your brain hear about it afterwards.
